title: The Hasmoneans
hookLine: the rebels became kings, and later rabbis were wary of their power

lines: EVERY MAN UNDER HIS FIG TREE.
cards: Words on brass. Near the end of the first book of Maccabees, the people of Jerusalem write their thanks on tablets of brass and set them on pillars on Mount Zion, honoring Simon, a son of Mattathias.
The book glows about his years: the land had peace, and every man sat under his own vine and fig tree, with no one to make him afraid.
So the people make Simon their leader and high priest, with a condition written into the decree: until a faithful prophet should arise.
The family of Mattathias, the Hasmoneans, now holds the sword, the Temple and the government. What does that much power do to a family of heroes?

teach.b: Years later, in the Talmud, the Hasmonean ruler is King Yannai, and he wears two crowns: the crown of a king and the crown of the high priest. Tractate Kiddushin tells a tense story.
Yannai comes home from a victory and throws a feast for the sages of Israel. At the table, one guest stirs him up, telling him the sages resent him.
Then an elder named Yehudah ben Gedidyah speaks, with the whole room listening: King Yannai, let the crown of kingship be enough for you. Leave the crown of priesthood to the descendants of Aaron.

Yannai, furious, turns on the sages and kills them, and the world is left desolate of Torah until Shimon ben Shetach restores it. Mattathias's sons risked everything so that no king could force his will on the Temple.
Their descendants end up as kings the sages feared.

teach.h: OIL AND LIGHTS, NOT A THRONE.
teach.b: Some readers think that's why, when the Talmud asks what Hanukkah is, it answers with a jar of oil and the lights, not a throne.
Another passage, in tractate Berakhot, tells of a high priest named Yochanan who served faithfully for many years and changed at the end.
The Talmud ties it to Hillel's warning from Pirkei Avot: do not trust in yourself until the day of your death. The power that rescues can become the power that crushes, sometimes within one family.

how: Students of Pirkei Avot learn Hillel's warning, do not trust in yourself until the day of your death, and the Talmud's stories of King Yannai and of Yochanan the high priest are studied in tractates Kiddushin and Berakhot.

o: the sages King Yannai killed at his victory feast
the family of Mattathias, rescuers who later became kings
the Greek kings who ruled Judah after Alexander

p: let the crown of kingship be enough

s: Simon was made high priest with no conditions
the decree in 1 Maccabees says: until a faithful prophet should arise.
in the Talmud, a sage told King Yannai to give up the priestly crown
Yehudah ben Gedidyah said: let the crown of kingship be enough; leave the priesthood to the descendants of Aaron.
the Talmud teaches that a good leader can't go wrong
Berakhot tells of a high priest who changed at the end, and cites Hillel: do not trust in yourself until the day of your death.

games.q: you're a sage at King Yannai's feast. he wears both crowns, king and high priest. the room is watching. what do you say?
o: let the crown of kingship be enough; leave the priesthood to Aaron's descendants.
games.why: in tractate Kiddushin, Yehudah ben Gedidyah says it out loud. the story says Yannai turns on the sages in his anger.

practice: Think of a moment you had a little power, a promotion, being the oldest sibling, being right in an argument, and look honestly, without judging, at how you used it.

Then think of one person you admire who now holds power, and wish them the wisdom of Yehudah ben Gedidyah's line: let one crown be enough. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition to stay faithful to who you were.

wordCard.voice: The Hasmoneans. The family of Mattathias, who rescued the Temple, and whose descendants became kings the rabbis were wary of. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Hasmonean, the family name of Mattathias and his descendants, used in the Hanukkah prayer Al HaNissim.

carryVoice: Your line: heroes can change. One crown can be enough. Day eight hundred ninety-four, done.
